topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: Physical health in serious mental illness
blurb: Close the mortality gap: baseline and follow-up checks on antipsychotics, the six-part annual health check and smoking cessation.
question: Joel, 23, started olanzapine 4 weeks ago for first-episode psychosis. He has gained 5 kg and says he wants to stop smoking. What should the community nurse do?

teach.body: People with serious mental illness (SMI: schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and other psychoses) die on average 15 to 20 years earlier than the general population, mostly from preventable physical illness such as heart and lung disease. Antipsychotics, smoking, inactivity and diagnostic overshadowing all add to the risk. Plain English: for many people with SMI, the illness most likely to shorten their life is physical, so mental health nurses must 'not just screen, but intervene'.
teach.cite: OHID premature mortality in SMI; NHS England 2024 (updated 2025)

teach.h: Smoking and clozapine or olanzapine levels
teach.body: Smoking tobacco speeds up the liver's breakdown of clozapine and olanzapine. If someone stops or cuts down, levels of these drugs can rise, causing sedation or toxicity. NICE CG178 says offer help to stop smoking even if earlier attempts failed, be aware of this effect, and do not offer bupropion to people with psychosis. Warn people on varenicline about neuropsychiatric effects and monitor closely in the first 2 to 3 weeks.

items: Do the baseline checks before the first antipsychotic dose and record them.
Watch for diagnostic overshadowing: chest pain, breathlessness or weight change are physical until proved otherwise.
Ask about constipation on clozapine, and about sexual side effects and periods (prolactin).
Share results with primary care, the care coordinator and the psychiatrist.

teach.body: Joel is in the weekly-weighing period, and 5 kg in 4 weeks is rapid gain. The nurse charts his weight, checks that baseline bloods were done, and offers a combined healthy eating and activity programme. She tells the prescriber so the medicine can be reviewed. She welcomes his wish to stop smoking, refers him for support (not bupropion), and flags that his olanzapine level may rise when he stops, so his team can review for sedation.

teach.text: Stopping smoking is good, but it can RAISE clozapine and olanzapine levels: tell the prescriber before or when someone quits. And bupropion is not offered to people with psychosis to help them stop smoking (CG178), even though it is a standard option for other people.

items: SMI shortens life by 15-20 years, mainly through preventable physical illness.
Annual check: alcohol, smoking, BMI, BP, glucose or HbA1c, lipids.
Antipsychotics: baseline checks; weight weekly for 6 weeks, then 12 weeks, 1 year, yearly.
Offer smoking cessation; stopping raises clozapine and olanzapine levels; no bupropion in psychosis.

summary: You can now explain the SMI mortality gap and carry out the six-part annual health check. You can also schedule antipsychotic monitoring, act on rapid weight gain and support stopping smoking safely on clozapine or olanzapine.

A.q: Which is one of the six core elements of the annual physical health check for people with serious mental illness in England?
A.why: The six elements are alcohol consumption, smoking status, BMI, blood pressure, blood glucose or HbA1c, and lipid profile (NHS England).

whyNot.0: Thyroid tests are needed for lithium monitoring, not the six core elements.
whyNot.2: A full blood count is needed for clozapine monitoring, not the core six.
whyNot.3: Peak flow is not one of the six elements.

A.q: How often does NICE CG178 advise weighing a person in the first 6 weeks after starting an antipsychotic?
A.why: CG178 1.3.6.4: weight weekly for the first 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks, at 1 year and then annually, plotted on a chart.

whyNot.0: Daily weighing is not the CG178 schedule.
whyNot.1: Monthly would miss rapid early gain.
whyNot.2: 12 weeks is the next check after the weekly period.

A.q: On average, how much earlier do people with serious mental illness die than the general population?
A.why: People with SMI die on average 15 to 20 years earlier, mostly from preventable physical illness.

B.q: Mrs Adeyemi, on clozapine, tells you she stopped smoking 5 days ago. She is now drowsier than usual. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Tell the prescriber; her clozapine level may be rising
Advise her to restart smoking until her next clinic visit
Reassure her that this is expected nicotine withdrawal
Advise her to take her clozapine every other day for now
B.why: Stopping smoking reduces clozapine metabolism, so levels can rise and cause sedation or toxicity (CG178 1.1.2.3). The prescriber needs to review, often with a plasma level.

whyNot.1: The answer is dose review, not restarting smoking.
whyNot.2: New drowsiness on clozapine after quitting needs medical review, not reassurance.
whyNot.3: Dose changes must come from the prescriber.

B.q: A man with schizophrenia wants medication to help him stop smoking. Which option does NICE CG178 advise against for people with psychosis?
options: Behavioural support from a stop-smoking service
B.why: CG178 1.1.2.4: do not offer bupropion to people with psychosis to help them stop smoking.

whyNot.3: Combination NRT is a standard option.

B.q: Before Ms Clarke starts her first antipsychotic as an inpatient, which baseline set does NICE CG178 require?
options: Weight, waist, pulse, BP, glucose, lipids, prolactin and ECG
Weight and blood pressure, then bloods after 12 weeks
Full blood count, liver tests and urine drug screen
Lithium level, thyroid and kidney function
B.why: CG178 1.3.6.1-1.3.6.2: weight, waist, pulse and BP, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, prolactin, movement disorders and nutrition; an ECG is offered on inpatient admission.

whyNot.1: Bloods are part of the baseline, not delayed to 12 weeks.
whyNot.2: These are not the CG178 antipsychotic baseline.

C.q: Aisha, 31, with bipolar disorder, comes to the CMHT with chest pain and breathlessness. A colleague says 'she gets panic attacks' and suggests breathing exercises. What should the nurse do?
options: Start breathing exercises and review her in an hour
Give her prescribed PRN lorazepam for the anxiety
Assess her physically and escalate for medical review
Book a GP appointment for later in the week
C.why: Assuming new physical symptoms are psychiatric is diagnostic overshadowing; people with SMI have higher cardiovascular risk, so assess (for example NEWS2, ECG) and escalate.

whyNot.0: This delays assessment of possible cardiac or respiratory causes.
whyNot.1: Sedation could mask a physical emergency.
whyNot.3: Chest pain with breathlessness needs prompt assessment, not a later appointment.

C.q: Joel's 12-week review on olanzapine shows rapid weight gain and raised fasting glucose. Which response fits NICE CG178?
options: Recheck everything at the planned 1-year review
Accept it as an expected side effect of olanzapine
Offer interventions and review with the prescriber
C.why: CG178 1.1.2.2: rapid or excessive weight gain or glucose problems call for interventions in line with NICE guidance, and the medicine should be reviewed with the prescriber.

whyNot.0: Waiting a year leaves metabolic harm untreated.
whyNot.1: Expected does not mean acceptable; NICE says intervene.
whyNot.2: Stopping abruptly risks relapse; changes are planned with the prescriber.

C.q: Mr Byrne has been stable on an antipsychotic for 18 months. The CMHT wants to transfer his physical health monitoring to his GP. What does NICE CG178 say?
options: Transfer is allowed after 5 years of stability
Monitoring can now stop if he is stable
Transfer under shared care, with checks at least yearly
The CMHT must keep monitoring indefinitely
C.why: CG178 1.3.6.5 and 1.5.3.2: secondary care monitors for at least 12 months or until stable, whichever is longer, then may transfer to primary care under shared care, where the GP checks physical health at least annually.

whyNot.0: The CG178 minimum is 12 months or until stable, not 5 years.
whyNot.1: Stability does not end monitoring: after transfer the GP checks physical health at least annually (1.5.3.2).
whyNot.3: Transfer to primary care is allowed after the initial period.

reteach.title: Screen, then act
reteach.question: What turns a physical health check into better health?

blocks.body: Recording a weight or a glucose result changes nothing on its own. NICE and the Lester resource ask nurses to act: offer healthy eating and activity programmes, stop-smoking support, and a medicine review when weight, glucose or lipids move the wrong way.

blocks.text: Quitting smoking can push up clozapine and olanzapine levels.

explain.body: Alcohol consumption, smoking status, BMI, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c, and lipid profile, checked at least once a year.

test.q: Which item is NOT among the six core elements of the SMI annual health check?
test.why: The six elements are alcohol, smoking, BMI, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c and lipids.

whyNot.0: Smoking status is a core element.
whyNot.1: Alcohol consumption is a core element.
whyNot.2: Blood pressure is a core element.

explain.body: Weight weekly for 6 weeks, then 12 weeks, 1 year, yearly. Pulse, BP, glucose and lipids at 12 weeks, 1 year, yearly. Waist annually.

test.q: When does NICE CG178 advise checking glucose and lipids after an antipsychotic is started?
test.why: CG178 1.3.6.4: fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks, at 1 year and then annually.

whyNot.1: Weekly applies to weight in the first 6 weeks.
whyNot.2: 3-monthly lifelong testing is not the CG178 schedule.
whyNot.3: 6 months and 2-yearly are not CG178 time points.

explain.body: Offer help to stop even after failed attempts; stopping raises clozapine and olanzapine levels; no bupropion in psychosis; monitor closely for 2-3 weeks on varenicline.

test.q: Which antipsychotics does NICE CG178 name as particularly affected when a person cuts down smoking?
test.why: CG178 1.1.2.3: be aware of the impact of reducing smoking on the metabolism of other drugs, particularly clozapine and olanzapine.

whyNot.0: These are not the drugs CG178 names.
whyNot.2: These are not the drugs CG178 names.

explain.body: Attributing physical symptoms to mental illness delays diagnosis. Assess physical complaints in people with SMI as you would anyone else's, and escalate.

test.q: A man with schizophrenia reports new abdominal pain. A colleague says it is 'one of his delusions'. What does this illustrate?
options: Somatic delusion that needs no action
test.why: Assuming a physical complaint is part of the mental illness is diagnostic overshadowing, a cause of missed physical illness in SMI.

whyNot.1: A physical complaint needs assessment before any psychiatric explanation.
whyNot.2: This is an assumption, not an assessed side effect.
whyNot.3: Labelling symptoms this way is stigmatising and unsafe.
